section.title: Elihu's Second Speech
section.sectionRationale: Elihu turns from addressing Job personally to defending God's justice as a general principle, answering Job's charge that God has denied him justice. He argues that a God who governs the whole earth impartially, showing no favoritism to princes over paupers, cannot possibly act wickedly, and he grows increasingly harsh toward Job, accusing him of speaking without knowledge and adding rebellion to his suffering.
section.thesis: Elihu rightly insists that the Judge of all the earth cannot act unjustly, since injustice would undo the very order that holds the world together, but he wrongly assumes this settles the specific question of Job's own suffering, and his closing harshness shows he, too, can overreach.
section.frameNote: Four movements: Elihu's summons to the wise to judge Job's words; his declaration that God, far from God to do wrong, governs with perfect justice; his description of God's impartial sovereignty over kings and commoners alike; and a hypothetical scene of repentance followed by Elihu's harsh verdict that Job has added rebellion to his sin.

verses.text: Then Elihu continued:
“Hear my words, O wise men; give ear to me, O men of learning.
For the ear tests words as the mouth tastes food.
Let us choose for ourselves what is right; let us learn together what is good.
For Job has declared, ‘I am righteous, yet God has deprived me of justice.
Would I lie about my case? My wound is incurable, though I am without transgression.’
What man is like Job, who drinks up derision like water?
He keeps company with evildoers and walks with wicked men.
For he has said, ‘It profits a man nothing that he should delight in God.’

units.label: Far be it from God to do wrong
units.note: He repays according to a man's deeds

verses.text: Therefore listen to me, O men of understanding. Far be it from God to do wrong, and from the Almighty to act {{rasha|wickedly}}.
For according to a man’s deeds He repays him; according to a man’s ways He brings consequences.
Indeed, it is true that God does not act wickedly, and the Almighty does not pervert {{mishpat|justice}}.
Who gave Him charge over the earth? Who appointed Him over the whole world?
If He were to set His heart to it and withdraw His Spirit and breath,
all flesh would perish together and mankind would return to the dust.
If you have understanding, hear this; listen to my words.
Could one who hates justice govern? Will you condemn the just and mighty One,
who says to kings, ‘You are worthless!’ and to nobles, ‘You are wicked,’
who is not {{panim|partial}} to princes and does not favor rich over poor? For they are all the work of His hands.
They die in an instant, in the middle of the night. The people convulse and pass away; the mighty are removed without human hand.
For His eyes are on the ways of a man, and He sees his every step.
There is no darkness or deep shadow where the workers of iniquity can hide.
For God need not examine a man further or have him approach for judgment.
He shatters the mighty without inquiry and sets up others in their place.
Therefore, He recognizes their deeds; He overthrows them in the night and they are crushed.
He strikes them for their wickedness in full view,
because they turned aside from Him and had no regard for any of His ways.
They caused the cry of the poor to come before Him, and He heard the outcry of the afflicted.
But when He remains silent, who can condemn Him? When He hides His face, who can see Him? Yet He watches over both man and nation,
that godless men should not rule or lay snares for the people.
Suppose someone says to God, ‘I have endured my punishment; I will offend no more.
Teach me what I cannot see; if I have done wrong, I will not do it again.’
Should God repay you on your own terms when you have disavowed His? You must choose, not I; so tell me what you know.
Men of understanding will declare to me, and the wise men who hear me will say:
‘Job speaks without knowledge; his words lack insight.’
If only Job were tried to the utmost for answering like a wicked man.
For he adds {{pesha|rebellion}} to his sin; he claps his hands among us and multiplies his words against God.”

rasha.gloss: To act wickedly, to do wrong. Elihu insists it is unthinkable, 'far be it,' that God would act this way, an important true premise that he then applies with more confidence than the situation warrants.

mishpat.gloss: Justice, judgment, the right ordering of a case. Elihu argues God cannot pervert mishpat, since He governs the whole earth; the question the book leaves open is whether this truth explains Job's specific suffering or simply restates a premise Job never actually denied.

panim.gloss: Literally 'to lift the face,' an idiom for showing partiality or favoritism. Elihu insists God is not partial to princes over paupers, since all are equally 'the work of His hands,' a genuinely important biblical truth about God's impartial justice, Deuteronomy 10:17.

pesha.gloss: Rebellion, transgression, willful revolt, often distinguished from unintentional sin. Elihu's final accusation that Job 'adds rebellion to his sin' is his harshest charge yet, treating Job's protest of innocence as active defiance against God rather than honest lament.

basic.context: Elihu shifts from addressing Job personally to arguing a general theological point before an imagined audience of wise men: God cannot possibly be unjust, since He governs the whole world impartially, showing no favoritism between kings and commoners. He grows harsher as he goes, eventually accusing Job of adding rebellion to his suffering by continuing to protest his innocence.
basic.hermeneutics: Elihu's core claim, that God is not and cannot be unjust, is true and important; the flaw is in the application, assuming that Job's charge of being 'denied justice' must therefore be false pride rather than honest confusion from a man who genuinely does not understand why he is suffering. True theology applied without listening can still wound.
basic.originalLanguages: Elihu insists it is unthinkable that God would rasha, act wickedly, or pervert mishpat, justice, since He shows no nasa panim, partiality, between rich and poor. Yet his conclusion, that Job has added pesha, rebellion, to his suffering, shows Elihu himself overreaching into a harsh verdict the narrative does not actually support.
basic.typology: Elihu's insistence that God judges impartially, seeing every deed and hearing every cry of the oppressed, anticipates the New Testament's teaching on a final impartial judgment executed through Christ, who judges the world in righteousness, Acts 17:31.
basic.christ: Elihu rightly says God 'need not examine a man further' since His eyes are already on every step, a truth fully realized in Christ, who is entrusted with all judgment because the Father has given Him authority as the Son of Man, John 5:22, 27; every deed done in darkness will be exposed before Him.
basic.god: God's justice truly is impartial, as Elihu insists, not favoring rich over poor, king over commoner; yet the same book that contains Elihu's confident speech will soon show God speaking to Job not with a philosophical defense of His impartial justice but with an overwhelming display of His wisdom and power, redirecting the whole question.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 10:17 describes God as showing no partiality and accepting no bribe. Acts 17:31 announces a fixed day of righteous judgment through Christ. John 5:22, 27 gives Christ authority to judge. Romans 2:11 states plainly that God shows no favoritism.
basic.oneStory: Elihu's true claim that God judges impartially, seeing every hidden deed, anticipates the final judgment secured through Christ. Yet the chapter also shows how even true theology, spoken with too much certainty about someone else's pain, can slide into harsh judgment rather than help; only Christ's judgment is perfectly matched to perfect knowledge and perfect love.

context.literary:
Elihu's second speech changes his audience. In chapter 33 he spoke to Job. In Job 34:2 he turns to a jury: "Hear my words, O wise men; give ear to me, O men of learning." From then on Job is spoken about in the third person, and the speech has the feel of a case being argued in front of the elders at the gate. The opening sets the terms in a proverb, "the ear tests words as the mouth tastes food," Job 34:3, and Job himself had said nearly the same thing in Job 12:11. Elihu is borrowing Job's own standard of judgment and turning it on him.

The movement is clear. Verses 5 to 9 give Job's alleged words and Elihu's verdict that he keeps company with the wicked. Verses 10 to 15 set out the thesis that God cannot do wrong, and that all life hangs on His breath. Verses 16 to 30 ask whether one who hates justice could govern, and answer with a survey of God's rule over kings and nations, with the eye that sees every step and the strength that topples the mighty in a night. Verses 31 to 33 are a hypothetical repentance, and they are among the hardest verses in the chapter to translate, with English versions differing on who is speaking and how. Verses 34 to 37 close with a verdict, that Job speaks without knowledge and adds rebellion to his sin.

There is a rhetorical pattern in the questions. Verses 13, 17, 18 and 29 ask who could rival God, who could condemn Him, or who could judge Him. Those questions are built to have one answer, "no one." The most sting comes in Job 34:36, where Elihu wishes that Job "were tried to the utmost." A reader who has just come from Job 1 and 2 knows that he already has been.
context.historical:
The picture of a wise assembly is drawn from life. Legal and political questions were decided by elders at the gate of a town, where cases were heard and public opinion mattered, and Job himself remembers sitting there in Job 29:7-10. Elihu speaks like a man laying out an argument before that body. Because Job is not being addressed, the speech does more to show Job as a case than to speak to him as a person.

The heart of the argument is the belief that a king is answerable to no earthly judge and yet God stands above kings. Elihu's language about nobles and princes, Job 34:18-20, would have been heard in a world of absolute rulers who were seldom checked. To say that God tells kings "You are worthless" and does not favour rich over poor was to say that the ordinary law of favour and bribe does not reach heaven. The same conviction was written into Israel's law: the LORD shows no partiality and accepts no bribe, Deuteronomy 10:17, and a judge must remember that there is no injustice or partiality with the LORD, 2 Chronicles 19:7.

The line that "all flesh would perish together and mankind would return to the dust," Job 34:15, assumes the picture of Genesis 2:7 and 3:19, in which breath from God gives life and its withdrawal ends it. Psalm 104:29-30 uses the same picture.

Sudden death at midnight was a recognised sign of divine judgment, as in the tenth plague of Exodus 12:29. Elihu says the mighty are removed "in the middle of the night," Job 34:20, and overthrown "in the night," Job 34:25. He is describing a God whose justice can act without warning.
context.canonical:
The claim that God cannot do wrong is basic to Scripture. Abraham stands before the LORD over Sodom and says, "Far be it from You... Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?" Genesis 18:25. Elihu's opening use of "Far be it" in Job 34:10 makes the same appeal. Bildad had asked the same question in Job 8:3, "Does God pervert justice?" Elihu answers it with a firmer yes to the doctrine and with a harder edge against the sufferer.

The theology of impartiality is repeated throughout the Bible. Deuteronomy 10:17 and 2 Chronicles 19:7 name it in the law, Acts 10:34 has Peter say that God does not show favoritism, and Romans 2:6-11 uses the same fact to level Jew and Greek, saying that God will repay each one according to his deeds. Proverbs 24:12 and Psalm 62:12 make the same statement about repayment.

Yet the Bible also holds this doctrine in tension. Ecclesiastes 8:14 records righteous men who get what the wicked deserve, and Psalm 73 wrestles with the prosperity of the godless until the psalmist enters the sanctuary and discerns their end, Psalm 73:16-17. Job 21 has already made this argument. Jesus refuses the inference in Luke 13:1-5 and John 9:1-3.

The New Testament carries Elihu's true point forward into the last judgment. God has set a day when He will judge the world in righteousness by the Man He has appointed, Acts 17:31, and the Father has given all judgment to the Son, John 5:22-27. 2 Corinthians 5:10 says everyone must appear before the judgment seat of Christ. Elihu's claim that no darkness can hide the workers of iniquity, Job 34:22, is echoed in the New Testament's claim that nothing is hidden.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer of Job uses this speech to press one question harder than any before it: if God is just, what may a sufferer say? Elihu answers with a doctrine that is sound and a verdict that is not. He is right that God does not pervert justice, Job 34:12, that no one appointed Him over the earth, Job 34:13, and that He sees every step, Job 34:21. These lines belong in the book, and the LORD will not contradict them.

But the writer wants the reader to feel the distance between the truth and the way it is used. Elihu has just heard a man who lost his children, health and standing, and he says Job "drinks up derision like water," Job 34:7, and "keeps company with evildoers," Job 34:8. He wishes Job were "tried to the utmost," Job 34:36, when Job 1 and 2 have shown that he was. Readers hold information that Elihu does not, and the gap between what we know and what he says is the writer's method.

The first hearers were meant to leave with two things. God's justice is not in doubt, and yet no one may use that justice as a stick against a hurting person. It prepares the ground for the whirlwind speeches, where the LORD does not defend His justice to Job in the terms Elihu expects, but asks whether Job would really annul it, Job 40:8.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Job 34 records Elihu's argument. It does not command that we speak about God or about sufferers in this way. The statements about God's character, that He is not partial, that He sees everything and that He does no wrong, are affirmed elsewhere in Scripture and can be taught with confidence, Deuteronomy 10:17 and Romans 2:11. The statements about Job, that he is wicked, rebellious and proud, are Elihu's judgment, not God's, and the book's ending disagrees with the spirit of them, Job 42:7.

The application is careful listening. When someone in distress speaks sharply about God, it is quite possible to be right about doctrine and wrong about the person. Elihu's fault is not that he defends God. It is that he assumes Job's protest must be sin, when Job 1:22 and 2:10 have shown a man who has kept faith. Christians may defend God's justice without pretending to know why a particular person is suffering. A fitting response to such a protest is closer to the Psalms, which allow complaint to become prayer.

debates.question: Is Elihu's central claim, that God cannot do wrong, the book's answer to Job?

views.label: Yes, it is the book's teaching
views.case: The LORD never says Job was right to say God had deprived him of justice, and He asks in Job 40:8, "Would you really annul My justice?" The claim that God is just is the ground under all the book's wisdom. Elihu is defending that claim, and the LORD does not contradict it.

views.label: No, it is true but not the answer
views.case: The LORD's speeches do not take up the question of justice as Elihu frames it. He never explains Job's suffering, and Job 42:7 says Job spoke of Him accurately while the friends did not. The book wants readers to see that a true doctrine used as a whole account of a sufferer's case is not the answer.

debates.bearing: The two answers fit together. God's justice is settled by the book, as Job 40:8 shows, but the book will not let it be used as a tool to explain each person's pain. Elihu says something true and then draws a conclusion the book refuses.

debates.question: Does Elihu quote Job fairly?

views.label: Fairly, in substance
views.case: Job did say God had deprived him of justice, Job 27:2, and had spoken of God's arrows against him, Job 6:4. Elihu picks the right themes.

views.label: Unfairly, by stretching
views.case: Job never says it profits a man nothing to delight in God (Job 34:9). The nearest words are those Job attributes to the wicked in Job 21:14-15, and he adds in Job 21:16 that he stays far from their counsel. Job also speaks of God as one who sees his steps in Job 31:4, so he does not deny what Elihu says in Job 34:21.

debates.bearing: Elihu's summaries begin as fair, then drift toward a caricature. That drift is a warning about how easily we accuse a sufferer of holding views that they have only voiced in pain.

study.originalLanguages:
Elihu begins with a proverb about the senses in Job 34:3, that the ear tests words as the mouth tastes food. The verb "tests" is bachan, the assay of metals and the testing of hearts, used for the LORD's own testing in Psalm 26:2 and Jeremiah 17:10. Job used the same picture in Job 12:11. To test a word is to weigh it before swallowing it. Elihu invites the wise to do that with Job's speech, which is fair, and then does not do it himself.

The phrase "Far be it from God" in Job 34:10 is a formula of horror, the same used by Abraham in Genesis 18:25 when he says "Far be it from You." It is a way of saying that a thought is beyond thinking. Job 34:12 repeats the point with a pair of verbs: God does not act wickedly and does not pervert justice. The word for justice here is mishpat, the word for the right ordering of a case, and it is the same word Bildad used in Job 8:3 and that the LORD uses in Job 40:8. The debate of the whole book circles around this one word.

Three words for wrong-doing meet in the chapter, and Elihu is careful about the order. Job's alleged sin is chatta'ah, a missing of the mark, and what he adds to it is pesha in Job 34:37, rebellion or breach of relationship. The prophets use pesha for Israel's revolt against the LORD, as in Isaiah 1:2, and Psalm 32 puts chatta'ah, pesha and avon (iniquity) side by side, Psalm 32:1-2 and 32:5. Job himself used the word in Job 7:21 when he asked why God did not pardon his transgression. Elihu says that Job's speech is not honest confusion but revolt, which is a very heavy word.

The phrase in Job 34:19 that God is "not partial to princes" is literally that He does not lift the face. To "lift a face" is to show favour, and the same idiom stands behind Deuteronomy 10:17, "showing no partiality." The reason given is the same as Job's in Job 31:15: they are all the work of His hands. In Job 34:14-15 the withdrawal of God's "Spirit and breath" from all flesh uses the same pair of ruach and neshamah that Elihu used in chapter 33 and that Genesis 2:7 uses of creation. Life is on loan, and Psalm 104:29-30 says the same.

The verse that God "need not examine a man further" in Job 34:23 has a legal ring: God has no need to set a time for a trial, since He already knows. It stands in some contrast to Genesis 18:21, where the LORD says He will go down and see whether the outcry is as bad as reported. Scripture speaks both ways, of a God who knows all things and of a God who condescends to inquire so that His justice can be seen.

Verses 31 to 33 are notoriously hard, and English translations divide over who says what. The BSB reads them as a hypothetical prayer, "Suppose someone says to God, 'I have endured my punishment; I will offend no more,'" followed by Elihu's retort that God will not repay on Job's terms. Readers should treat the verses with caution and rely on the clearer sentences around them.

Finally, "claps his hands" in Job 34:37 describes a gesture of scorn. Job 27:23 uses it of an enemy who claps his hands at a fallen man. Elihu says Job does this "among us," treating Job's speech as mockery of God.

typology.type: The impartial Judge who sees every step, Job 34:19-23
typology.fulfillment: Elihu describes a Judge who shows no favour to kings or the rich and whose eyes are on every step. The Bible teaches that this judgment is placed in the hands of a man. God has set a day to judge the world by the Man He appointed, Acts 17:31, and the Father has given all judgment to the Son, because He is the Son of Man, John 5:22 and 5:27. Christ fulfils the type by adding what Elihu could not: the Judge shares our nature and took our place, Hebrews 4:15. The type falls short because Elihu's Judge acts from a distance and without inquiry, while Christ came near and was tried.

typology.type: The man wrongly condemned by the wise, Job 34:34-37
typology.fulfillment: Elihu asks the wise to join him in saying, "Job speaks without knowledge," and wishes him "tried to the utmost." A righteous sufferer is called a rebel and a scoffer by the learned. The pattern fits Christ in a deeper way. The leaders condemned Him, and Peter says they rejected the Holy and Righteous One, Acts 3:14. Where Job was misjudged by men who did not know his heart, Jesus is the sinless One who suffered without sin, 1 Peter 2:22-23, and entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly. Job falls short as a type because he was not sinless, Job 42:6, and the Servant is.

typology.type: Life held in God's breath, Job 34:14-15
typology.fulfillment: If God withdrew His Spirit and breath, all flesh would perish and return to the dust. The picture of life sustained moment by moment by God reaches its answer in Christ, who is life in Himself, John 5:26, and who breathed on His disciples and said, "Receive the Holy Spirit," John 20:22. In Him the breath is given as new life, not merely borrowed. The type falls short because Elihu's picture is of fragility and warning, while the gospel adds that the life given in Christ cannot be withdrawn, Romans 8:38-39.

study.christ:
Job 34 leads to Christ most directly through the judge. Elihu's God cannot be bribed, is not partial, sees every step and needs no long inquiry. Those are features of the last judgment as the New Testament describes it, and Acts 17:31 adds that God will judge "by the Man He has appointed" and has given proof by raising Him from the dead. John 5:22-27 says the Father has assigned all judgment to the Son and given Him authority to execute it "because He is the Son of Man." The judge who knows every step is also the one who took on flesh and walked our steps. Hebrews 4:15 says He was tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin, so that His judgment is neither cold nor naive.

Second, the chapter leads to Christ by contrast. Elihu wants Job to be "tried to the utmost," as though the most severe trial fit the most rebellious man. The New Testament shows the most severe trial falling on the one man who did not deserve it. He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth, and when they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate, 1 Peter 2:22-23. He was condemned by the learned, and Acts 3:14 records that they rejected the Holy and Righteous One. Elihu's question in Job 34:17, "Will you condemn the just and mighty One?", was meant as a rebuke to Job, but it names exactly what men did to Jesus, and the verdict they gave was wrong.

Third, the chapter points to Christ where it fails. Elihu insists there is no way to accuse God. But Job's longing in Job 9:33, for someone who can lay a hand on both God and himself, is not addressed here. Elihu has a Judge and no mediator in this chapter, whereas the previous chapter had a mediator. The gospel joins the two, since the one who will judge is also the one who gave Himself as a ransom, 1 Timothy 2:5-6. The final verdict is therefore not a verdict to fear for those who trust in Him. John 5:24 says whoever hears His word and believes "will not come under judgment."

Fourth, Elihu says God sees "every step" and no darkness can hide a wrongdoer, Job 34:21-22. That is a threat if standing alone. In Christ it becomes a promise for the sufferer, since the One who sees every step is the one who suffered for us. Romans 2:16 says God will judge people's secrets through Christ Jesus, and 2 Corinthians 5:10 says all must appear before His judgment seat.

A caution is needed. Elihu says nothing about Christ, and the typology should not run wild. The link holds because the New Testament itself gives the judgment of God to the Son, and because the book's ending vindicates the righteous sufferer whom the wise misjudged.
study.god:
Elihu is right about a good deal in this chapter, and any account of the doctrine of God should say so first. God does not do wrong. The Almighty does not pervert justice, Job 34:12. He owes no account to any higher power, since no one gave Him charge over the earth, Job 34:13. He holds every living thing in being, so that if He withdrew His Spirit and breath, all flesh would perish, Job 34:14-15. These three claims teach the goodness, the sovereignty and the sustaining care of God, and Scripture affirms each of them elsewhere, for example in Psalm 104:29-30 and Acts 17:25.

The chapter also shows God's impartiality. He is not partial to princes and does not favour rich over poor, "for they are all the work of His hands," Job 34:19. It is a doctrine that lifts the poor and warns the powerful. Job himself believed it, which is why he could ask in Job 31:15 whether the same God did not make his servants. Deuteronomy 10:17 and Romans 2:11 give the same teaching.

God is presented as the one who sees. "His eyes are on the ways of a man, and He sees his every step," Job 34:21. Job had said the same in Job 31:4. It is a comfort to the oppressed, who cry out and are heard, Job 34:28, and a warning to the wicked, who cannot hide in any darkness, Job 34:22.

There is a tension in the way the chapter speaks of God's silence. Elihu says that when God remains silent, no one can condemn Him, and when He hides His face, no one can see Him, Job 34:29. This is true as far as it goes: God owes us no explanation. But Job was in exactly this situation, and to say "no one can condemn Him" is very different from saying "no one should cry out." The Psalms show that a faithful person can complain of God's hidden face and still trust Him. The LORD in the end speaks, and the silence is broken.

The chapter does not tell us the deepest thing about God, that His justice and mercy meet at the cross. Romans 3:25-26 says God presented Christ as an atoning sacrifice "to be just and to justify" the one who trusts in Jesus. The chapter teaches worship in this way: to bow before a God who is right in all He does, and to take care that our confidence in His justice never becomes a weapon against the hurting. A fitting response is the prayer of Psalm 51:4, that God is proved right when He speaks and blameless when He judges.

crossReferences.note: Abraham appeals to the same certainty as Elihu, "Far be it from You," and asks whether the Judge of all the earth will not do what is right. In Genesis the question is a plea for mercy on the righteous. In Job 34:10 the same conviction is turned into an argument against the sufferer. The comparison shows how one doctrine can be prayed or used as a stick.

Job says the ear tests words as the tongue tastes food. In Job 34:3 Elihu adopts the proverb as his own standard. The echo shows that Elihu is answering Job on Job's terms, and it invites the reader to test Elihu's words by the same rule.

Bildad asks whether God perverts justice. Elihu's Job 34:12 repeats the point almost word for word. It shows Elihu covering ground the friends have already covered, and it is a reminder that a true proposition can be used badly by more than one speaker.

Job says the same God who made him made his servants, and that he will answer to God for how he treated them. Elihu's remark in Job 34:19 that rich and poor are alike the work of God's hands is therefore one Job already believed. The passage undercuts the claim that Job denies God's impartiality.

Job asks whether God does not see his ways and count his every step. Elihu says in Job 34:21 that God sees a man's every step. The two men agree, which makes it striking that Elihu treats Job as a denier of what he actually affirmed.

The wicked ask what they would gain if they prayed, and Job answers that he stays far from their counsel. Elihu's quotation in Job 34:9, that it profits nothing to delight in God, sounds like the wicked's words, not Job's. It shows how a sufferer can be credited with what he explicitly rejected.

The LORD asks Job whether he would annul His justice and condemn Him to justify himself. This answers Elihu's concern in Job 34:17, and it shows that the LORD takes seriously the danger Elihu names, while dealing with it in His own way.

The LORD shows no partiality and accepts no bribe. This is the law's form of Elihu's teaching in Job 34:19, and it grounds his words in the covenant God of Israel, not in a general idea of divine fairness.

Paul says God will repay each one according to his deeds and that He does not show favoritism. He uses Elihu's principle to remove any Jewish claim to be safe from judgment. The teaching is true, but it leaves everyone guilty and prepares the way for the gospel of Romans 3.

God has set a day to judge the world with justice by the Man He appointed, and proved it by raising Him from the dead. The impartial Judge of Job 34 is here identified, and the resurrection guarantees that the judgment is real.

The Father has assigned all judgment to the Son, who has authority to judge because He is the Son of Man. Elihu's God who needs no further inquiry is here joined to the human Saviour who shares our life. Verse 24 adds the good news that believers will not come under judgment.

Jesus refuses to say that those killed by Pilate or by the falling tower were worse sinners than others. It is the New Testament's plain correction of the habit that Elihu shows, of reading a person's suffering as a verdict on their character.

study.oneStory:
From the garden onward the Bible is a story about who will judge and whether the judge can be trusted. In Genesis 3 the serpent sows the suspicion that God is not fair, and the man and woman step out of trust. Genesis 18:25 asks whether the Judge of all the earth will do right. Elihu's speech is one of the fullest replies in the Old Testament, with a statement that God is just, impartial, all-seeing and the source of every breath. It looks back to the creation that the first chapters describe, where breath from God gives life, and it insists that the story of the world is not in the hands of chance or of rival powers.

What the chapter sets up is the tension the rest of Scripture must resolve. If God is perfectly just, how can sinners stand before Him? Elihu's answer, that God repays a man according to his deeds, Job 34:11, is affirmed by Romans 2:6, and it is exactly what makes the gospel necessary. Ecclesiastes and Psalm 73 show the problem from the side of experience, where the just seem to suffer and the wicked prosper. The prophets promise a day when the crooked will be made straight.

The chapter also shows a danger inside the story: true theology in the mouth of one who does not listen. Job's friends, and then Elihu, keep the doctrine and lose the person. Jesus repeats the lesson in Luke 13:1-5 and John 9:1-3.

The story comes to its answer in Christ. The judge is a man, Acts 17:31, and this man took the punishment His own verdicts require, so that God could be "just and the one who justifies," Romans 3:26. The wise of this world condemn the righteous, as Elihu wished on Job, and God raises the righteous. Isaiah 53:11 speaks of a righteous Servant who justifies many.

In the new creation the Judge's justice is not a threat but a joy. The tears are wiped away, and there is no more mourning or crying or pain, Revelation 21:4. The oppressed whose cry reached God, Job 34:28, are answered, and the God who is not partial to the wise or the powerful welcomes into His presence everyone whose name is written in the Lamb's book of life, Revelation 21:27.

sermon.title: Job: Rebuked in Suffering
sermon.why: Piper's sermon on Job 32:1-37:24 treats the whole of Elihu's speeches together, including this defense of God's impartial justice in chapter 34, framing Elihu's rebuke of Job's presumption as a preparation for God's own address to Job from the whirlwind.

quiz.q: What is Elihu's central claim in 34:10-15?

options.text: It is unthinkable for God to act wickedly or pervert justice, since He sustains and governs all creation.
options.note: Verses 10-12 state this directly, with verses 14-15 grounding it in God's sustaining power over all life.

options.text: God sometimes acts unjustly but should not be questioned about it.
options.note: Elihu's whole argument is that God cannot act unjustly at all, not that injustice is permissible but unquestionable.

options.text: Justice is a purely human concept that does not apply to God.
options.note: Elihu applies the concept of justice directly to God, arguing He perfectly embodies it, not that it is irrelevant to Him.

options.text: God's justice mainly works through the moral order built into creation, functioning almost automatically.
options.note: Close to Elihu's broader argument, but he specifically stresses God's direct, personal governance and attention, not merely an impersonal built-in order.

quiz.q: What does Elihu mean when he says God is not 'partial to princes,' 34:19?

options.text: God treats the powerful and the powerless with equal justice, since both are equally His creation.
options.note: Verse 19 grounds this impartiality in the fact that all people are 'the work of His hands.'

options.text: God favors kings and rulers over ordinary people.
options.note: Elihu says the opposite; God shows no such favoritism.

options.text: God has no interest in how nations are governed.
options.note: The surrounding verses show God actively removing unjust rulers, 34:24-25, showing real interest in governance.

options.text: God judges powerful rulers only when their wrongdoing becomes extremely severe.
options.note: Close, God does judge rulers, but Elihu's point is that God's justice is constant and impartial, not triggered only by extreme severity.

quiz.q: What is Elihu's final, harshest charge against Job in 34:36-37?

options.text: That Job has added rebellion to his sin, multiplying words against God without knowledge.
options.note: This is Elihu's most severe accusation in the speech, wishing Job would be 'tried to the utmost.'

options.text: That Job has never sinned at all.
options.note: Elihu's accusation is the opposite, that Job's continued protest constitutes active rebellion.

options.text: That Job's friends were entirely correct in their earlier speeches.
options.note: Elihu has separately criticized the three friends for failing to actually refute Job, 32:3.

options.text: That Job should simply stop speaking and quietly accept his suffering.
options.note: Close to the spirit of Elihu's frustration, but his actual charge is sharper and more specific: that Job's continued protest amounts to willful rebellion, not merely too much talking.

quiz.q: How does the epilogue in 42:7-8 relate to Elihu's charge that Job rebelled by speaking without knowledge?

options.text: God's verdict names only the three friends as having spoken wrongly, not repeating Elihu's specific charge against Job as rebellion.
options.note: This suggests Elihu's harsh conclusion here outran what the book itself ultimately affirms about Job.

options.text: God gently corrects Job's presumption in the whirlwind speeches, though without ever calling it rebellion the way Elihu does.
options.note: True and close, God does correct Job's presumption in chapters 38-41, but 42:7-8 specifically vindicates Job's speech over the friends', stronger than Elihu's harsh charge allows.

options.text: God condemns Elihu by name alongside the three friends.
options.note: Elihu is notably absent from the list of those God rebukes, which is itself significant, though the text does not explicitly praise him either.

options.text: The epilogue never mentions Job's earlier speeches at all.
options.note: 42:7-8 directly references what Job and the friends 'spoke' about God, engaging their speeches directly.

quiz.q: How does Elihu's picture of God's impartial, all seeing justice anticipate the New Testament?

options.text: It anticipates the final, impartial judgment of all people entrusted to Christ.
options.note: Acts 17:31 and John 5:22, 27 develop exactly this theme of impartial judgment given to the Son.

options.text: It teaches that judgment will never actually occur.
options.note: Elihu's whole point is that God's judgment is active and inescapable, a theme carried forward into final judgment.

options.text: It shows that only the wealthy will be judged by God.
options.note: Elihu's point is the opposite, that rich and poor are judged with equal impartiality.

options.text: It mainly reflects ancient legal ideals about kings, with only loose connection to New Testament teaching on judgment.
options.note: Partly true about the ancient background, but the impartial, all seeing judgment Elihu describes maps directly onto Acts 17:31 and John 5:22, 27, a real anticipation, not merely a loose connection.

questions: Elihu was right that God cannot be unjust, but he applied that truth harshly to a suffering man. Where might you need to hold a true belief with more gentleness toward someone who is hurting?
Elihu insists God shows no favoritism between rich and poor. Are there ways you unconsciously treat some people's concerns as more important to God than others?

Elihu accuses Job of rebellion for continuing to protest his innocence, yet God later says Job spoke rightly. What helps you tell the difference between honest lament and actual rebellion against God in your own life?
God's justice is impartial and all seeing, nothing done in darkness escapes Him. Does that truth comfort you or unsettle you more right now, and why?
Elihu's true theology, applied without enough humility, became harsh. Think of a time someone corrected you with truth but without gentleness. How did it land, and what would you have needed instead?

translationNotes.note: 'The ear tests words as the mouth tastes food' is a proverbial image for careful discernment, inviting Elihu's audience to weigh his argument rather than accept it uncritically.
'Without human hand' describes sudden deaths attributed directly to God's action rather than to any visible human agent, emphasizing His unmediated sovereignty over life and death.

'When He remains silent, who can condemn Him' captures Elihu's argument that God's inscrutability itself is proof no one is qualified to judge His ways, an idea that anticipates the tone, though not the specific content, of God's own speech in chapters 38-41.
